2. Value-at-Risk & Expected Shortfall

Four VaR models on the same portfolio. Fat tails show up as Cornish-Fisher and Student-t Monte Carlo VaR exceeding the normal (parametric) figure at high confidence.

Backtest: are the VaR models any good?

Every forecast uses only data available the day before (500-day window). Exceptions are tested with Kupiec's proportion-of-failures test (right number of breaches?) and Christoffersen's independence test (are breaches clustered?).

ModelObservationsExceptionsExpectedException RateKupiec p-valueIndependence p-valueCond. Coverage p-valueLast-250d ExceptionsBasel ZoneVerdict
Historical43804943.8001.12%0.4380.0000.0002GreenFAIL
Parametric43807343.8001.67%0.0000.0000.0003GreenFAIL
EWMA43809643.8002.19%0.0000.0060.0006YellowFAIL
Filtered HS43805543.8001.26%0.1020.0010.0012GreenFAIL

Historical VaR gets the count right (49 vs 43.8 expected, Kupiec p=0.44) but its breaches cluster in crises (independence p=0.000) because a 2-year window reacts slowly. EWMA reacts fast but assumes normal tails, so it breaches far too often (96 exceptions). Filtered Historical Simulation combines both ideas. It has 55 exceptions (Kupiec p=0.10) and reduces clustering, but clustering is still statistically significant (p=0.001). Crises like 2008 and March 2020 produce back-to-back breaches that no 1-day model fully anticipates, which is exactly why VaR is paired with the stress tests below. (Parameters were left at the RiskMetrics standard, λ=0.94, rather than tuned to pass the test.)

Hypothetical scenarios (1-month horizon)

Rate scenarios use the recent correlation regime. Since 2022, stocks and bonds have been positively correlated, so a rates shock now hurts equities too. Calibrating on crisis-era data (when Treasuries rallied as stocks fell) would wrongly show a rates shock as a gain.
